records.title: Governance: establish adversarial convergence protocol before Child C
Epic: Simplify agent orchestration for deterministic development
records.body:
## Epic Goal and User Value
Make coding fast and deterministic by ensuring requirements, technical decisions, file scope, dependencies, and validation commands are resolved before Development begins; remove duplicate orchestration ownership and replace arbitrary handoffs with one explicit, bounded workflow contract.

## Product Brief

### Problem
The user reports that agent files and orchestration patterns overcomplicate tasks, cause excessive handoffs, and leave too much ambiguity by Development. They expected coding to be fast and deterministic by that phase.

### Evidence & Research
- Codebase: the installed plugin source shows competing pipeline narratives in `README.md`, `agents/orchestrator.agent.md`, and `agents/dispatcher.agent.md`; Development is a routing hub in `agents/development.agent.md`; return paths overlap across `agents/architecture-security.agent.md`, `agents/standards.agent.md`, `agents/reviewer.agent.md`, `agents/quality.agent.md`, and `agents/platform-ops.agent.md`. Existing canonical policy assets include `skills/github-issue-tracking/SKILL.md`, `skills/implementation-plan-format/SKILL.md`, `skills/parallel-safety-check/SKILL.md`, and `skills/quality-gate-checklist/SKILL.md`. No standalone orchestration test suite was found.
- Technical: contract-first handoffs, explicit workflow graphs, deterministic validation, bounded recovery, and minimum necessary transitions are supported by [Microsoft Agent Framework handoff guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/orchestrations/handoff), [Microsoft Conductor](https://opensource.microsoft.com/blog/2026/05/14/conductor-deterministic-orchestration-for-multi-agent-ai-workflows/), [Salesforce Agent Script](https://engineering.salesforce.com/agentforces-agentscript-building-deterministic-control-for-enterprise-ai-workflows/), and [Bandara et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08769).
- Market/competitive: not applicable; this is internal developer-workflow remediation rather than a user-facing market feature.

### Proposed Scope
Establish one authoritative machine-readable orchestration contract and accessible guide; add an offline deterministic validator and CI contradiction fixtures; align planning/dispatch, architecture/standards, Development, review/quality, and integration/deployment agent definitions; preserve GitHub issue tracking and both human approval checkpoints.

### Explicitly Out of Scope
Application/product-code changes, a new agent framework, wholesale agent replacement, automatic wave dispatch, branch-protection administration, production deployment, and changes to the two human approval gates.

### Constraints & Assumptions
- Remote is `jmassardo/agentic-sdlc`; the checkout currently contains only `.git`, while the installed plugin source provides the repository-relative paths used in child plans.
- Every child is one concern, at most one competent-agent workday, one reviewable PR, and includes its own validation.
- Python 3.11+ standard library is sufficient for offline validation; no new runtime dependency is planned.
- Existing agents are simplified rather than replaced.
- No due date was provided, so Milestone 1 has no due date.
- No implementation or dispatch is authorized until the human approves this breakdown.

### Success Metrics
- Exactly one documented happy path and bounded recovery graph.
- 100% of declared handoffs have one canonical owner/reason and match the contract.
- Development has one complete entry contract, one normal Reviewer exit, and zero ownership of upstream decisions or routing arbitration.
- All seeded contradiction classes fail deterministic offline validation; valid repository input passes.
- Both human approvals remain mandatory and auditable.
- A maintainer identifies next owner and recovery owner for five supplied states within 60 seconds each.

## Epic Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Given an implementation-ready atomic issue, when it enters Development, then all behavior, file scope, technical/security decisions, dependencies, and validation commands are resolved and Development performs implementation only.
- [ ] Given any declared handoff or recovery path, when repository validation runs, then it matches one canonical transition owner, reason, status effect, retry limit, and approval requirement.
- [ ] Given a gate failure with retry capacity, when recovery occurs, then it follows the declared bounded path; on exhaustion it becomes `status:blocked` with `needs-human`.
- [ ] Given dispatch or merge to main lacks recorded human approval, when the workflow reaches that checkpoint, then progression stops.
- [ ] Edge case: Given Standards is unnecessary, deployment is inapplicable, or approved direct single-issue handoff avoids batching, when the workflow runs, then the explicit conditional or terminal path applies without an invented handoff.
- [ ] Error case: Given an unknown agent, duplicate transition owner, inconsistent phase/retry, missing approval, undeclared handoff, or

records.title: Materialised state has no cache — every `ls` re-replays the whole log (twice)
records.body:
## Summary

The materialiser currently has no persisted cache. Every consumer call (`ls`, `cat`, `exists`, `listFiles`, `listDirectories`, `watchVolume` delta, every HTTP read in the eventual app) triggers a full pipeline:

1. `openChannel(secret)` — derive keypair
2. `loadEventLog(volume, log)` — read every `channels/<pubkey>/<eventHash>.bin` from disk
3. `verifyEventLog(entries, volume)` — re-verify every signature
4. `materialize(canonical)` — sort by `(timestamp, log-position, eventHash)` + single-pass fold

The output is plain `Map<string, FileMetadata>` etc. allocated per call, returned, used once, and garbage collected before the next prompt returns. There is **no** in-memory cache, **no** on-disk cache, **no** snapshot.

A glaring example today: the REPL's `ls` calls `listFiles` and `listDirectories` *in parallel* and **each** does the full pipeline independently:

```ts
const [files, dirs] = await Promise.all([
  ctx.fileService.listFiles(secret),
  ctx.fileService.listDirectories(secret),
]);
```
(`src/cli/commands.ts`)

```ts
async function listFilesWithDeps(...) {
  const volume = await openChannel(normalizeSecret(secret), crypto);
  const entries = await loadEventLog(volume, channelStorage, crypto);
  await verifyEventLog(entries, volume, crypto);
  return materializeFilesFromEntries(entries);
}

async function listDirectoriesWithDeps(...) {
  const volume = await openChannel(normalizeSecret(secret), crypto);
  const entries = await loadEventLog(volume, channelStorage, crypto);
  await verifyEventLog(entries, volume, crypto);
  const fs = materialize(toCanonicalEntries(entries));
  return [...fs.directories.values()].sort(...);
}
```
(`src/fileService.ts`)

So each `ls` keystroke does the full open + read + verify + sort + fold **twice** concurrently. Fine for a 5-event toy volume; awful as soon as the log grows.

## Why it hurts (and where it doesn't yet)

| Scenario | Pain level |
|---|---|
| Toy volumes (< 100 events), interactive REPL | invisible — terminal redraw dominates |
| Reactive UI subscribed to volume changes | every event triggers full re-fold; visible jitter as log grows |
| HTTP `GET /files` on a hot path in `nearbytes-app` | every request pays O(N) replay; throughput-bound |
| First sync of a large existing volume | every newly-arrived event triggers a fresh full re-fold of the entire log |
| Volumes with 10⁴–10⁶ events | linear in log size every keystroke |

The cost is also doubled by the unnecessary double-replay in the REPL `ls` path, and the verify pass is the dominant cost beyond a few hundred events (signature verification is ~order-of-magnitude more expensive than the materialiser fold itself).

## Easy wins (independent of the bigger question)

These don't require any architectural changes and could ship today:

- **`Promise.all([listFiles, listDirectories])` → one combined materialise call.** Eliminates the 2× factor in the REPL `ls` immediately.
- **In-process memoisation.** Cache `(volume, lastEventHash) → MaterializedFileSystem`. Invalidate when a new event lands (sync delivers an event for this channel, or `addFile/mkdir/delete/rename` is called locally). Reduces every read after the first to O(1) until the log mutates. Pure in-memory, no on-disk surface.

These two together probably address 95% of the actual pain for current volume sizes.

## The bigger question: persistent cache

For real-world scales (and to survive process restart without paying the cold-load cost) the right move is a persistent indexed cache. The natural fit is SQLite, encrypted with the volume secret. Trade-off space we worked through:

### Option A — SQLite as event store + materialiser-in-code (recommended)

- One table: `events(event_hash PK, timestamp, log_position, type, path, from_path, to_path, blob_hash, encrypted_key, ...)` with indexes on `(timestamp, log_position, event_hash)`, `path`, `from_path`, `to_path` (prefix-friendly).
- The events table replaces the current `channels/<pubkey>/*.bin` per-file storage at the *cache* layer (the log on disk remains the durable source of truth; the SQLite cache is rebuildable from it at any time).
- `ls` etc. still pass events through the in-code materialiser, but:
  - SQL gives indexed slices of events relevant to a query (path prefix, time range), not the full log.
  - Atomic single-row INSERTs for new events from sync.
  - Late events (timestamps earlier than current cursor) are just INSERTs; the cache is rebuilt from scratch at sync-session boundary, not per event.
- Code-level result caching (LRU keyed by `(query_shape, max_event_hash)`) sits on top.
- **Cascade semantics live in exactly one place** (the materialiser), so the v0.4 spec → code correspondence stays 1-to-1.

### Option B — SQLite as event store + cascade in SQL views (rejected for v0.4)

- Same events table.
- `live_files`, `live_directories`, etc. expressed as SQL views with recursive CTEs that re-derive the cascade per query.
- Pure event-sourcing, no derived tables.
- Rej

records.title: Persist and resume Local Markdown Reduce batches
records.body:
# OpenWiki Local Markdown Reduce batch checkpoint/resume Spec

- Date: 2026-08-13
- Status: **Final Candidate Revision 2**
- Scope: `src/local-markdown` Reduce execution and its SQLite journal
- Evidence baseline: current source/tests plus `/tmp/openwiki-reduce-checkpoint-ledger-audit-20260813.md`

## 1. Outcome

Deepen the existing Reducer module so every successfully validated Reduce batch is durably journaled before execution can cross the next batch boundary. After interruption or process restart, the compiler deterministically reconstructs the same Reduce tree, reuses committed nodes, and calls the model only for the current outcome-unknown node and later pending nodes.

The feature preserves one provider/model identity per compile request and does not introduce fallback, racing, parallel reduction, or a second model seam.

The intended zero-call behavior is deliberately narrow:

1. An unchanged snapshot with a current, verified publication continues to use the existing publication fast path: `mapCalls=0`, `reduceCalls=0`.
2. A crash after final Reduce commit but before successful publication finalization resumes from the retained checkpoint: `mapCalls=0`, `reduceCalls=0`, followed by normal integrity checks, staging, validation, and atomic publication.
3. After publication is successfully recorded and the run is finished, every Reduce checkpoint scope in that source's ledger is cleared. A later stale marker or tampered page therefore preserves current behavior: `mapCalls=0`, `reduceCalls>0`.

## 2. Compatibility baseline

The following are fixed compatibility contracts:

- `LOCAL_MARKDOWN_PLANNER_VERSION` remains `"3"`.
- `createChunkId()` and `createShardId()` inputs and outputs remain unchanged.
- Existing Map receipt compatibility remains exactly `createCompatibilityKey({ provider, model, promptVersion, plannerVersion })`.
- Existing receipt status, artifact JSON, source reference, adaptive Map split, and lookup behavior remain unchanged.
- Normal resume does not rewrite a legacy-v3 plan or add `planId`, packing, or checkpoint metadata to that file.
- The read-time derived `planId` for a legacy-v3 plan remains stable and is used only in the new Reduce checkpoint scope.
- Managed publication marker stays version 2 with its current shape and validation rules.
- Atomic generation/pointer publication stays unchanged.
- Existing `LocalMarkdownCompileReport` required fields and `counts.reduceCalls` semantics stay unchanged.
- Existing boundary cancellation stays unchanged: both Map and Reduce call the model adapter with `signal: undefined`.

The currently running 4,588-document legacy-v3 UAT is planned to be cut over after implementation and copied-state gates pass. During development, candidate code, tests, and delegated development agents must not open, migrate, lock, stop, or call a provider against its live source/state/wiki roots. The authorized main UAT controller may continue the existing read-only health checks and may create one transactionally consistent SQLite online backup plus immutable-snapshot copies for isolated copied-state testing. No migration or test command may run against the live originals.

## 3. Module and interface

### 3.1 External seam: unchanged

```ts
compileLocalMarkdown(
  request: LocalMarkdownCompileRequest,
): Promise<LocalMarkdownCompileReport>
```

No checkpoint token, global state directory, resume handle, or new required report field is exposed.

The existing model interface is also unchanged:

```ts
LocalMarkdownModelAdapter.reduce({
  artifacts,
  batchId,
  level,
  signal,
  snapshotId,
}): Promise<{ artifacts: LocalMarkdownArtifact[] }>
```

For every Reduce provider call, `signal` remains `undefined`. The production adapter continues to create its own 20-minute timeout signal internally.

### 3.2 Internal Reducer module

Keep one internal interface and deepen its implementation, for example:

```ts
reduceArtifacts({
  artifacts,
  counters,
  ledger,
  limits,
  request,
  scope: { compatibilityKey, planId, runId, snapshotId },
}): Promise<LocalMarkdownArtifact[]>
```

The Reducer module owns all of the following:

- existing ordered partitioning and 12-level termination;
- canonical artifact hashes and durable node IDs;
- stable provider-visible batch labels;
- completed/split node lookup and validation;
- source reference merging;
- output validation;
- retry and adaptive split decisions;
- node commit before cancellation boundary;
- level barrier transaction;
- final checkpoint reuse and invalidation.

`compiler.ts` supplies the scope and consumes final artifacts. It must not construct node IDs, drive Reduce SQL states, or interpret split lineage.

SQLite remains an internal dependency of the existing ledger module. Do not add a global-home storage seam or a new public repository interface. Narrow internal ledger operations may be added for opening a job, reading a node, committing a node/job transition, invalidating the terminal node, and deleting a scope.

```text
VIB.FIV.FLOW_TURBULENCE
```

Parent family gate: #429 — Vibration & Dynamic Screening.

Current editable-input implementation baseline: PR #442 — `feat(vibration): add editable FIT benchmark input tables`.

Related future mechanism: #441 — AIV takeover specification.

This issue is the **expert takeover specification** for completing FIT. A new agent must be able to execute the remaining work without reconstructing conversation history.

Target engineering maturity:

```text
Traceability target          >= 95%
Engineering/software quality >= 95%
Engineering UI maturity      >= 92%
Overall workspace maturity   >= 94%
```

These are engineering maturity targets, not automated-test coverage percentages.

---

# 0. Authority freeze

Current FIT authority remains:

```text
calculationState       = IMPLEMENTED
qualificationState     = BENCHMARK_ONLY
engineeringAuthority   = NONE
screeningAuthority     = NOT_AUTHORIZED
designAuthority        = false
```

Do **not** promote FIT to screening/design authority in this issue unless all independent engineering qualification gates are closed and the Owner explicitly approves the authority transition.

This takeover may improve traceability, editable-input handling, evidence, benchmarking, reproducibility, diagnostics, testing and UX. It must not invent or silently modify FIT equations, coefficients, empirical correlations, applicability rules, thresholds or authority semantics.

Any discovered method defect must be logged as `ISS-*` / `QST-*`, source-reconciled and fail closed.

records.title: Optimize the performance of RzGraph and related structures implementation and algorithms
Performance metrics refactor: PSYPD/QSYPD rename, overlap-aware critical-path metrics, caching and test experiments
records.body:
# Performance metrics refactor: PSYPD/QSYPD rename, overlap-aware critical-path metrics, caching and test experiments

## Context (for readers new to Autosubmit)

This branch reworks those metrics and adds a new family based on the workflow's
critical path. The performance report is served by:

```
GET /v3/performance/<expid>
```

defined in `autosubmit_api/routers/v3/experiments.py`. All the metric maths lives
under `autosubmit_api/performance/`.

---

## 1. What was developed

### 1.1 Metric rename: ASYPD -> PSYPD (backward compatible)

`ASYPD` (Autosubmit SYPD) was renamed to **PSYPD** (Parallel SYPD) everywhere.
`ASYPD` is still emitted in every response as an exact alias of `PSYPD`, so no
existing consumer breaks. Touched files:

- `autosubmit_api/performance/performance_metrics.py`
- `autosubmit_api/performance/utils.py` (`calculate_ASYPD_perjob` kept as alias of
  `calculate_PSYPD_perjob`)
- `autosubmit_api/components/jobs/job_factory.py`
- `autosubmit_api/components/representations/graph/graph.py`
- `autosubmit_api/components/representations/tree/tree.py`
- `autosubmit_api/history/experiment_history.py`

### 1.2 New metric: QSYPD

**QSYPD** (Queue SYPD) measures SYPD against run time plus queue time, without the
post-processing term. It exists both experiment-wide (in the performance report)
and per job (in the graph/tree representations, via
`calculate_QSYPD_perjob` in `autosubmit_api/performance/utils.py`).

### 1.3 Overlap-aware critical-path engine

A new engine in `autosubmit_api/performance/utils.py` computes the longest
(most expensive) path through the job dependency graph. It is:

- **Overlap-aware**: when a child job starts before its parent finished, only the
  non-overlapping part of the child is charged. Three primitives capture this:
  `runtime_overlap`, `queue_overlap` and `interruption` (idle gap between a parent
  finishing and the child being submitted).
- **Strategy-based**: three weightings, layered on top of each other:
  - `runtime` -> running time only,
  - `queue_runtime` -> running + queue,
  - `interruption_queue_runtime` -> running + queue + idle gaps (the full span).
- **Linear, O(V + E)**: a topological longest-path relaxation (Kahn's algorithm).
  The three weightings share a single in-degree computation, and the per-chunk
  sub-graphs are built once and reused.

The path is traversed from the graph roots (jobs with no dependency) down to the
leaves.

### 1.4 New workflow-level metrics: WSYPD / WQSYPD / WISYPD

SYPD measured against the overlap-aware critical path instead of the naive sum of
all SIM run-times:

- **WSYPD** = simulated years / critical-path running time,
- **WQSYPD** = ... / critical-path running + queue time,
- **WISYPD** = ... / critical-path full span (includes idle gaps).

Because the critical path is a single chain (the real bottleneck) rather than the
sum of every parallel member, these values reflect the achieved parallel
throughput.

### 1.5 New chunk-level metrics: CSYPD / CQSYPD / CISYPD

The same three weightings applied to the single heaviest chunk (the chunk whose
internal work is the bottleneck), using that chunk's own simulated years. Useful
to see which chunk dominates.

### 1.6 Critical-path reports in the API response

The response now carries six report objects, one per metric above:

```
runtime_critical_path
queue_runtime_critical_path
interruption_queue_runtime_critical_path
runtime_chunk_critical_path
queue_runtime_chunk_critical_path
interruption_queue_runtime_chunk_critical_path
```

Each report lists the jobs on that path with their timestamps and per-job
overlap-aware weights, plus totals. This is what a UI needs to draw the path.

### 1.7 Performance caching

`autosubmit_api/routers/v3/experiments.py` now caches each computed report,
keyed on a version token `(pkl_last_modified, history_db_last_modified)`. If
neither the job list nor the historical timing DB changed, the whole computation
is skipped. Failed computations are never cached (they raise so nothing is
stored). For the largest experiment this turns a ~5-8 s cold computation into a
~0.02 s cache hit.

### 1.8 Tests

- `tests/test_critical_path.py` (new) - the engine, weightings, chunk paths,
  wrapper cases.
- `tests/test_performance.py` (extended) - the new metrics.
- `tests/test_performance_cache.py` (new) - the caching / version-token behaviour.

Run them with `pytest tests/test_critical_path.py tests/test_performance.py
tests/test_performance_cache.py`.

---

## 2. How to install and run it (automated)

A self-contained testbed is attached as **`autosubmit-api-testbed.zip`**. It
installs dependencies, generates the database files and the test experiments, and
runs the API. Contents:

- `setup.sh` - creates a virtualenv, runs `pip install -e .` on the repo
  (pulls every dependency, including Autosubmit itself), generates the three
  synthetic experiments and writes the config file.
- `run.sh` - starts the API on `http://127.0.0.1:8000` (interactive API docs at
  `

records.title: Release convergence: first-beta candidate execution
Exact Return: receipt-addressed artifact reconstruction across the Collective
records.body:
# Exact Return — receipt-addressed artifact reconstruction

## Felt possibility

The Haunted Toaster's render receipt is already becoming more than retrospective evidence. It binds an artifact to accepted score/timeline state, source identities, renderer/build provenance, and witnessed output.

The next possibility is larger:

> **A receipt should be sufficient authority and instruction to ask the Collective to make an artifact exist again.**

The Toaster becomes the first proving-ground executor for a network-level primitive rather than the owner of the primitive.

Core law:

> **Preserve causes. Regenerate consequences.**

A reconstructed artifact may be byte-identical, meaningfully equivalent, or only partially returnable. The receipt must say which claim it can actually support.

## Cross-stack shape

A reconstruction receipt may resolve through several project-owned authorities:

- **Project0** — canonical identities/addresses and relationships between artifacts, receipts, dependencies, and descendants.
- **TranchNode** — immutable/content-addressed source evidence and replayable dependency state.
- **Corpus OS** — admission, authority, historical interpretation, branches, human decisions, and exact routes back to evidence.
- **Haunted Toaster** — resolver/executor that walks the receipt graph, verifies dependencies, reconstructs, witnesses the result, and emits a new receipt.

The projects must keep their own authority. The Toaster may resolve and execute; it must not silently become the canonical store, historian, or authority plane.

## Receipt as portable capability

The receipt is the portable object a human carries between nodes.

Possessing a valid reconstruction receipt authorizes the holder/node to **request the reconstruction described by that receipt**.

It does **not** imply ambient authority over every protected dependency named inside it.

A protected dependency must be one of:

1. directly embedded / already available to the holder;
2. publicly or lawfully addressable immutable evidence;
3. reachable through a separate admitted capability/lease;
4. unavailable, in which case reconstruction degrades truthfully rather than bypassing authority.

This prevents the receipt from becoming a skeleton key while preserving its portability.

## Reconstruction graph

Conceptually:

```text
receipt
├── source identity
│   └── immutable artifact / hash
├── source identity
│   └── another reconstruction receipt
├── accepted specification / state
├── ordered transformations
├── dependency identities
├── execution environment
├── human-authoritative decisions
├── declared nondeterministic boundaries
└── expected result identity / equivalence claim
```

Resolution may recurse:

```text
receipt A
  -> needs artifact B
       -> receipt B
            -> immutable primitive C
  -> needs artifact D
       -> immutable TranchNode object
```

Every leaf must eventually resolve to either:

- an immutable primitive;
- another reconstructible receipt; or
- a declared irreducible external fact.

No hidden fourth category.

## Reconstruction classes

The receipt must declare the strongest return class it promises.

### EXACT RETURN

Same canonical inputs + deterministic execution environment produce the expected artifact identity/hash.

### LAWFUL RETURN

The same admitted specification and causal structure are reconstructed, but byte identity is not required or cannot be guaranteed. The receipt must define the equivalence/witness rule used.

### PARTIAL RETURN

Some irreducible dependency is unavailable. Everything recoverable is reconstructed, and the missing boundary is named explicitly.

A failed exact return must never be silently reported as lawful return without an explicit new disposition.

## Reconstruction result receipt

Every attempt emits a new receipt describing what actually happened, e.g.:

```text
requested: project0:artifact:...
requested-class: EXACT
resolved-dependencies: 47/47
recursive-reconstructions: 8
execution: deterministic
expected: sha256:...
observed: sha256:...
verdict: EXACT RETURN
```

or:

```text
verdict: LAWFUL RETURN
semantic/equivalence witness: PASS
byte identity: DIFFERENT
reason: declared encoder implementation variance
```

or:

```text
verdict: PARTIAL RETURN
missing irreducible source: physical microphone capture
all downstream reconstructible state preserved
```

## What must stay invariant

records.title: Category Module for AdultCMS
records.body:
# Category Module for AdultCMS

The Category module provides a comprehensive system for organizing and browsing content in the AdultCMS platform. This module enables hierarchical categorization of content with parent-child relationships, filterable category views, and SEO optimization.

## Features

- Hierarchical category structure (unlimited nesting levels)
- Category-based content filtering
- Category management in the admin panel
- AJAX-based category reordering
- SEO optimization with meta fields
- Frontend category browsing
- Multi-tenant support
- Soft deletion of categories

## Components

### Models

#### Category

The `Category` model implements the following features:

- Relations to parent/child categories
- Relations to content items
- Scopes for active, featured, and root categories
- Path building for breadcrumbs
- Tenant scoping for multi-tenancy
- Automatic slug generation

### Controllers

#### Admin\CategoryController

Administrative controller for managing categories with the following functionality:

- CRUD operations for categories
- AJAX-based category reordering
- Category filtering and search
- Authorization checks

#### CategoryController (Frontend)

Public-facing controller with the following features:

- Category listing and browsing
- Content filtering by categories
- Category tree API endpoint for frontend components

### Services

#### CategoryService

Service class that encapsulates business logic:

- Create, update, and delete operations with validation
- Prevention of circular references in parent-child relationships
- Category reordering functionality
- Tree structure building for hierarchical display

### Views

#### Admin Views

- `admin.categories.index` - List and manage categories
- `admin.categories.create` - Create new categories
- `admin.categories.edit` - Edit existing categories
- `admin.categories.show` - View detailed category information

#### Frontend Views

- `frontend.categories.index` - Browse all top-level categories
- `frontend.categories.show` - View a specific category and its contents
- `frontend.categories.filter` - Filter content by multiple categories

## Database Schema

### Categories Table

```
id (bigint) - Primary key
tenant_id (bigint) - Foreign key to tenants table
parent_id (bigint, nullable) - Self-referencing foreign key
name (string) - Category name
slug (string) - URL-friendly slug
description (text, nullable) - Category description
meta_title (string, nullable) - SEO meta title
meta_description (text, nullable) - SEO meta description
meta_keywords (string, nullable) - SEO meta keywords
icon (string, nullable) - CSS icon class
banner_image_id (bigint, nullable) - Foreign key to media table
is_active (boolean) - Whether category is active
is_featured (boolean) - Whether category is featured
sort_order (integer) - Order for sorting categories
color (string, nullable) - Color code for UI elements
settings (json, nullable) - Flexible settings storage
created_at (timestamp) - Creation timestamp
updated_at (timestamp) - Update timestamp
deleted_at (timestamp, nullable) - Soft delete timestamp
```

### Pivot Table: content_category

```
id (bigint) - Primary key
content_id (bigint) - Foreign key to contents table
category_id (bigint) - Foreign key to categories table
created_at (timestamp) - Creation timestamp
updated_at (timestamp) - Update timestamp
```

## Usage

### Admin Usage

#### Creating Categories

1. Navigate to `Admin > Categories > Create New`
2. Fill in the category details (name, description, etc.)
3. Optionally select a parent category for nesting
4. Upload an image if needed
5. Set status (active/inactive)
6. Add SEO metadata if needed
7. Click "Save"

#### Managing Categories

- Use drag and drop to reorder categories
- Filter categories by name, status, or parent
- Edit or delete categories as needed
- View subcategories and associated content

### Frontend Usage

#### Browsing Categories

Users can browse categories from the categories index page, navigating through the hierarchy to find content they're interested in.

#### Filtering Content

The filter page allows users to:
- Select multiple categories to filter content
- Sort results by newest, oldest, or most popular
- Paginate through filtered results

### API Endpoints

#### Category Tree

The `/api/categories/tree` endpoint returns a JSON representation of the category hierarchy, useful for building dynamic category browsers in the frontend.

## Extending the Module

### Adding Custom Fields

1. Add the field to the `categories` table
2. Add the field to the `$fillable` array in the `Category` model
3. Update the form views to include the new field
4. Add validation in the controller

### Adding New Category Types

To implement specialized category types (e.g., "Featured Sets"):

1. Add a `type` field to the `categories` table
2. Extend the Category model with scopes for the new type
3. Create specialized views for the new type
4. Implement any custom logic in the Cat
